item.title: Quickstart on Linux
item.description:
Go from nothing to a first job on one Linux node in five steps. The page sets up one class, linux-default, and installs nothing on the node by hand: a service of the stack installs the runner.

Note

This is a CircleCI Labs project, not supported by CircleCI support. It is a 0.x release: read the release notes before you upgrade. What is tested says how it is checked. One token proxy runs on a manager, so while it is down no new job starts: use three managers in production.

Before you start

  • A node with Ubuntu LTS, Docker Engine 24 or later, curl, a clock on NTP, and outbound HTTPS (what needs internet). Prepare each node shows how to install Docker.
  • The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, on your workstation or on the node.
  • An organization admin who accepted the CircleCI Runner Terms.
  • A runner namespace. If your organization has none, create one with circleci namespace create <NAMESPACE> --org <ORG>.

Replace <NAMESPACE> with your runner namespace, and <ORG> with your organization slug such as gh/my-org, or its UUID. Run the commands on the node as a user in the docker group, or add sudo.

Steps

  1. Create a resource class and a token. The command prints the token once: keep it for step 3.

    circleci auth login
circleci runner resource-class create <NAMESPACE>/linux-default --org <ORG> --generate-token

  2. On the node, download the latest release, and start a one-node Swarm that listens on the loopback address. To verify the release signature first, see Install on Linux > Verify a release.

    version=$(curl -fsSLI -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/latest)
version=${version##*/v}
curl -fsSL "https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v${version}/machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" | tar -xz
cd "machine-runner-swarm-${version}"
    sudo linux/setup.sh --check --swarm-init

    No other node can join this Swarm, and the runners share the node with the token proxy, so use it for a trial. For a cluster, follow Multi-Node Clusters instead.

  3. Create the secrets. The first command asks for the token from step 1 (hidden input). The token goes to the token proxy only. The second creates the placeholder that the runners read instead of a token.

    sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default
printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder

  4. Deploy the stack, and check it. docker stack deploy does not wait, so the replicas need a minute to start.

    sudo linux/setup.sh --deploy
    sudo docker stack services runners
circleci runner instance list --org <ORG> --resource-class <NAMESPACE>/linux-default

    The stack is up when runners_linux-default shows 2/2, runners_token-proxy shows 1/1, and the CLI lists an instance with the status online. If a replica stays Pending, the node is too small: it needs 4 CPUs and 8 GB, so set a lower deploy.replicas (Size the limits, A task stays pending).

  5. Run a job. Save this as .circleci/config.yml in a project of your organization, replace my-namespace with your namespace, then commit and push. The same file is examples/linux-hello.yml.

    version: 2.1

jobs:
 hello:
 machine: true
 resource_class: my-namespace/linux-default
 steps:
 - run:
 name: Show where this job runs
 command: |
 echo "runner: $CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME"
 if [ -e /tmp/hello-marker ]; then echo "the container was reused"; exit 1; fi
 touch /tmp/hello-marker
 echo "clean container: no marker from an earlier job"

workflows:
 hello:
 jobs:
 - hello

    Run the workflow twice. Both runs pass, because Swarm starts a new container for each job.

Next

  • Install on Linux: every step by hand, RHEL, release verification, and upgrades. Before production, copy linux/stack to a directory of your own and deploy that copy (Review the stack file).
  • Concepts: services as resource classes, the token proxy, and the job lifecycle.
  • Resource Classes: add classes, and change sizes and replicas.
  • Security: choose the default or the hardened class before you give a class to a team.
  • Operations: pin or roll back the runner, rotate tokens, and run the cluster.
  • Troubleshooting: symptoms, causes, and fixes.

item.title: Quickstart on Windows Server
item.description:
Go from nothing to a first job on one Windows Server node in five steps. Nothing is built or installed on the host: the stack uses the stock Server Core image, and a service of the stack installs the runner and Git.

Note

This is a CircleCI Labs project, not supported by CircleCI support. It is a 0.x release: read the release notes before you upgrade. What is tested says how it is checked. One token proxy runs on a manager, so while it is down no new job starts. This page sets up one host that runs the proxy and the jobs together: use it for a trial.

Before you start

  • A Windows Server 2022 or 2025 host (amd64, not a domain controller) with a clock on NTP and outbound HTTPS (what needs internet).
  • Docker Engine and CLI 28.0 or later in Windows-container mode, and the Windows Containers feature (Prerequisites shows how to install both). The first pull of the Server Core image is about 2.2 GB.
  • The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, on your workstation or on the host.
  • An organization admin who accepted the CircleCI Runner Terms.
  • A runner namespace. If your organization has none, create one with circleci namespace create <NAMESPACE> --org <ORG>.
  • An elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session on the host.

Replace <NAMESPACE> with your runner namespace, and <ORG> with your organization slug such as gh/my-org, or its UUID.

Steps

  1. Create a resource class and a token. The command prints the token once: keep it for step 3.

    circleci auth login
circleci runner resource-class create <NAMESPACE>/windows-default --org <ORG> --generate-token

  2. On the host, download the latest release. To verify the release signature first, see Install on Windows Server > Verify a release.

    $uri = (Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri 'https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/latest').BaseResponse.ResponseUri.AbsoluteUri
$version = $uri -replace '^.*/v', ''
$zip = "machine-runner-swarm-$version.zip"
Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v$version/$zip" -OutFile $zip
Expand-Archive -LiteralPath $zip -DestinationPath .
cd "machine-runner-swarm-$version"

  3. Pull the base image, then run the helper. Pull first: the network of the host drops for a few seconds after docker swarm init. The helper creates the Swarm, labels the node, asks for the token from step 1 (hidden input), creates the secrets, and deploys the stack. Use the IPv4 address of the host.

    docker pull mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022
    .\windows\Setup.ps1 -InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr <HOST_IPV4_ADDRESS> -Class windows-default -Deploy

  4. Check the stack. docker stack deploy does not wait, and the first start downloads the runner, so the replicas need a few minutes. Early runner tasks fail until the download ends, and Swarm restarts them.

    docker stack services runners
circleci runner instance list --org <ORG> --resource-class <NAMESPACE>/windows-default

    The stack is up when runners_windows-default shows 2/2 and the CLI lists an instance with the status online. If a replica stays Pending, the host is too small: each replica reserves 2 CPUs and 4 GB, so set a lower deploy.replicas (Size the limits, A task stays pending). docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows shows the install.

  5. Run a job. Save this as .circleci/config.yml in a project of your organization, replace my-namespace with your namespace, then commit and push. The file examples/windows-job.yml has more steps.

    version: 2.1

jobs:
 hello:
 machine: true
 resource_class: my-namespace/windows-default
 steps:
 - run: echo "computer $COMPUTERNAME, instance $MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_INSTANCE_ID"

workflows:
 hello:
 jobs:
 - hello

    Run the workflow twice. The two runs print different values, because Swarm starts a new container for each job.

What differs from Linux

  • A job runs as an administrator. The runner container holds a placeholder, and the class token stays in the token proxy, except in the windows-persistent class (Token model on each OS).
  • Stopping a busy container, for an update, a scale-down or a drain, kills its job after about 5 seconds. Change a class while it is idle (Stop a busy Windows container).

Next

  • Install on Windows Server: every step by hand, release verification, and upgrades. Before production, copy windows\stack to a directory of your own and deploy that copy (Review the stack files).
  • Concepts: services as resource classes, the token proxy, and the job lifecycle.
  • Images: add your own tools on top of Server Core.
  • Security: the token model and BitLocker.
  • Operations: upgrade, rotate tokens, and run the cluster.

item.title: Concepts
item.description:
The stack runs CircleCI machine runner 3 as Docker Swarm services. Swarm handles replicas, restarts, secrets, and placement. This repository adds a stack file for each operating system, a small entrypoint and a runner distributor service for Linux, and optional setup helpers. Read this page before you change a stack file or choose between the default and the hardened class.

Services are resource classes

Each Swarm service is one CircleCI resource class. The service name is the short name of the class, so the service linux-default serves the resource class <namespace>/linux-default. A job selects the class in its config:

jobs:
 build:
 machine: true
 resource_class: <namespace>/linux-default

Each service also has one Swarm secret, <service>-token, which holds the token of that class. In the single-task classes the token proxy holds it, and the runners hold a made-up placeholder. A persistent class mounts its token in the runner container itself.

flowchart TB
nodes["Nodes: Linux amd64, Linux arm64, Windows<br/>Labels decide where tasks may run"]
subgraph services["Swarm services: one for each resource class"]
direction LR
s1["linux-default<br/>replicas: 2"]
s2["linux-python<br/>replicas: 1"]
s3["windows-default<br/>replicas: 2"]
end
r1["container 1"]
r2["container 2"]
r3["container 1"]
r4["container 1"]
r5["container 2"]
api["runner.circleci.com<br/>Runners connect outbound over HTTPS 443 only"]
nodes --> services
s1 --> r1 & r2
s2 --> r3
s3 --> r4 & r5
r1 & r2 & r3 & r4 & r5 --> api

The runner containers poll CircleCI for work. Nothing connects to a runner, so the stack publishes no ports.

deploy.replicas is the number of runners in the class, and so the number of jobs it runs at the same time. A replica that fits on no node stays Pending until capacity is free. Resource Classes covers sizing.

The token proxy

The service token-proxy of runners.yaml (on Windows token-proxy-windows, which works the same way, with the differences in Windows) keeps the class tokens away from the runners and their jobs. A runner sends its API calls to the proxy (CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080) and holds only a placeholder token. The proxy adds the class token to one call, the task claim, and passes every other call on to CircleCI. The runner and its task agent use the task token from the claim response for the rest.

flowchart LR
subgraph cls["Class overlay networks"]
r1["linux-default runners<br/>placeholder token"]
r2["linux-python runners<br/>placeholder token"]
end
p["token-proxy<br/>one replica<br/>holds every class token"]
api["runner.circleci.com"]
r1 -- "claim, task calls" --> p
r2 -- "claim, task calls" --> p
p -- "HTTPS: the class token on the claim only" --> api

The network decides who may claim, not what a runner says. The proxy allows a claim only from an address that Swarm DNS lists now for tasks.<service> of a class, once for each container. A container that is not a runner, or a runner that claims a second time, gets 403. A claim whose outcome is unknown counts as a claim, so the proxy fails closed. The token proxy lists what it protects and what it does not, and Monitor the token proxy covers what happens when it is down.

What it changes for you:

  • Secrets. You create the class secrets <service>-token, and one more, runner-placeholder-token, with a made-up token. Only the proxy mounts the class secrets. Every runner mounts the placeholder.
  • Classes. A new single-task class needs two lines in the proxy: its network (Linux) and its secret <service>-token. See Resource classes. The persistent classes do not use the proxy.
  • The image. ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Docker Hub (the signature is the trust root, not the name): a static Go binary on a minimal base, with no shell. One tag covers Linux amd64, arm64, ppc64le and s390x, and Windows Server 2022 and 2025 (amd64). Swarm pulls it, and every digest is signed: The token proxy image, Verify the token proxy image.
  • The state. The proxy keeps the addresses of the runners that have claimed in the volume proxy-state, on the node that it runs on (a manager by default). If it moves, the state stays behind: Where the proxy runs, and when it moves. In a cluster, label the node machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run on a node with that label, so jobs do not share a node with the proxy. On a single node, set no label.

Add-on stack files and how they merge

Each operating system has one main stack file, runners.yaml, that defines the default classes and deploys on its own. Optional classes live in add-on stack files next to it:

File System Adds
persistent.yaml, docker-build.yaml, ssh-rerun.yaml Linux and Windows Persistent, Docker-build and SSH-rerun classes
custom-image.yaml Windows A class with your own image
microvm.yaml Linux MicroVM classes (MicroVM jobs)
container-mode.yaml Linux The prototype container agent for Docker-executor jobs (Container mode)

An add-on stack file is not a patch of the main file. It defines services of its own, and each service needs its own resource class and <service>-token secret. On Linux, docker-build.yaml, ssh-rerun.yaml, and microvm.yaml also add their classes to the token-proxy service, so deploy them together with runners.yaml. persistent.yaml and container-mode.yaml keep their own tokens and do not touch the proxy.

docker stack deploy -c runners.yaml -c persistent.yaml runners merges the files in the order given, as Docker Compose does for several -f files. A service, network, secret, or volume that only one file defines is added, and a key that several files set takes the value of the later file. YAML anchors work inside one file only, so each add-on stack file repeats the common service settings.

Pass the same files, in the same order, on every deploy: the services of a file you leave out stay as they are and stop following your edits, and --prune removes them. Check a merge without a Swarm with docker stack config -c runners.yaml -c persistent.yaml.

Single-task and continuous mode

The stack files set the runner mode with CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE.

Mode Value Behavior Environment
Single-task single-task (default in every stack file) The runner claims one job, runs it, and exits. Swarm starts a new container for the next job Clean for every job
Continuous continuous (persistent classes only) The runner stays up and claims job after job in the same container Shared by all jobs on that runner

Use continuous mode only for trusted projects that need warm caches: Persistent mode.

Job lifecycle

Swarm never reuses a container. Every exit (a finished job, an idle timeout, a crash) leads to a new task and a new container, because the restart policy is condition: any.

sequenceDiagram
participant S as Swarm
participant C as Container
participant A as runner.circleci.com
participant N as New container
S->>C: start a task from the image
C->>A: poll for a job (single-task mode)
A-->>C: claim one job
C->>C: run the job in a clean container
C-->>S: runner exits, container stops
Note over S: restart_policy any, delay 10s
S->>N: create a NEW task and container
N->>A: poll for the next job

On Linux the entrypoint checks the runner, sets up the users, and starts it, and the runner steps the job down to the job user. On Windows the runner is the main process. Timing:

  • A replica needs about 10 seconds (the restart delay) plus container start-up before it can claim the next job. The other replicas keep claiming in the meantime.
  • Every new container downloads the task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com. Allow this host in your egress rules.
  • A single-task runner that finds no job exits after CIRCLECI_RUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT (1h in the stack files), so idle replicas pick up a rotated secret or a new image within an hour.

Stopping a service sends SIGTERM to the runner. The runner drains: it accepts no new job and lets the running job finish. The stack sets stop_grace_period: 5h5m, the runner max_run_time of 5 hours plus 5 minutes.

On Windows, stop_grace_period does not hold a busy container: a stop from outside kills its job after about 5 seconds. An update, a scale-down, or a node drain is affected, so change a Windows service while its class is idle (Stop a busy Windows container).

What a clean environment covers

A clean environment means that a job starts in a container created from the image, with nothing left by an earlier job.

Covered Not covered
Files and installed packages anywhere in the container filesystem Anything on a mounted volume: persistent classes keep a named volume by design
The home directory, /tmp, and the working directory The Docker engine of the node when a class mounts its socket or named pipe: images, containers, and build cache persist
Processes, environment variables, and shell history State outside the node, such as databases, registries, and shared storage
Users, groups, and sudo rules created by an earlier job The kernel: all containers on a node share it
On Windows, the registry, the user profile, %TEMP%, and C:\ProgramData Data of finished containers that Swarm has not yet pruned from the node disk

The runner is mounted read-only, so a job cannot change what the next job runs (The runner distributor on Linux, The runner distributor on Windows). A single-task class needs no working directory cleanup, because the container is discarded. On Linux the runner does not clean it, because the runner user cannot remove files that the job user owns: the stack sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to "false" (Working directory cleanup).

Containers are not a virtual machine boundary. Read Security before you run untrusted code.

The runner distributor on Linux

The Linux services use stock images such as cimg/base, and the image holds none of the runner. The service runner-distributor puts the runner on every Linux node that runs the classes of runners.yaml. docker stack deploy is the whole install, and the only upgrade path.

  • The service. runner-distributor is a global service from the stock alpine:3 image (pinned by digest), so it runs on every Linux node, also a Docker-build node and a node that joins later. A microVM node (machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true) is the exception: the microVM classes download their own runner into each VM (MicroVM jobs). Its script, linux/stack/runner-distributor.sh, is a Swarm config.
  • The volume. It writes to runner-bin, one named volume on every node. Each version has a directory versions/<version> with bin/circleci-runner, SHA256, VERSION, and TARBALL. The link current points to the active version and moves with one atomic rename. The file history lists the versions in the order they were active.
  • The runner services. Every class mounts runner-bin read-only at /opt/machine-runner-swarm. The entrypoint is another Swarm config, mounted at /circleci-runner-entrypoint with the mode 0555. A job cannot change either.
  • The wait. The entrypoint waits up to MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_WAIT seconds (default 120) until current exists, so a first deploy and a new node need no order. Without a runner, or with a binary that differs from its record, it exits with code 80, and Swarm retries after the restart delay.

A container resolves current once, so a running job keeps its version and the next container gets the new one. A persistent class runs one container for all jobs, so it picks up a new version when its container restarts (Recycle a class). The runner services carry no version and no hash: the version is a setting of the distributor service only, so an upgrade, a pin, and a rollback change that one service, and the runner services never restart. An idle replica keeps the old binary until it recycles, within the idle timeout of 1 hour.

MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION Behavior
3.1.13 (an exact version, the default: the newest that CI tests) A pin. The tarball is checked against the SHA-256 values that the stack file carries for it, not the manifest. It never changes by itself, makes no request once installed, and switches to an installed version without network, so a rollback needs no download. A release of this repository bumps the version and its SHA-256 values together
3.1 or 3 A floating line: the newest 3.1.x, or the newest 3.x.y, of CircleCI’s manifest. Checked again every 24 hours. It ignores the default SHA-256 list and trusts the hash of the manifest, which is weaker
current CircleCI’s current release, within major version 3. Checked again every 24 hours, and trusts the manifest hash like the floating lines

See The version policy for the rules, how this compares with machine runner 3, container runner and the orchestrator, Upgrade the runner on Linux for the settings, and Runner binary integrity on Linux for the checks.

The runner distributor on Windows

The Windows services use the stock Server Core image, with none of the runner and none of Git. The service runner-distributor-windows does what the Linux distributor does, with the same settings and version policy.

  • The service. A global service on the nodes with the label machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022, from the stock servercore:ltsc2022 image with process isolation. Its script, windows\stack\runner-distributor.ps1, is a Swarm config.
  • The volume and the links. It writes to runner-bin: versions\<version> for the runner (with SHA256, TARBALL and VERSION), git\<git version> for portable Git, and two relative directory symbolic links, current and git\current. Every class mounts the volume read-only twice, with volume.subpath: current at C:\machine-runner-swarm, and git\current at C:\Program Files\Git, where the task agent expects tar.exe.
  • No entrypoint. circleci-runner.exe is the main process. A runner task that starts before the first flip fails and starts again after the restart delay, so a new node needs no order. Nothing checks the binary when a container starts: Runner binary integrity on Windows.
  • Locked files. Windows cannot replace or delete files that a running container uses. The distributor installs a version next to the others, flips the link, and removes an old version only when no container uses it. No busy job is killed by an upgrade.

See Upgrade the runner on Windows for the settings.

Users and the runner token on Linux

Inside each Linux container, two accounts exist:

  • The runner user circleci-runner (uid 2000) runs circleci-runner and owns the token file. It has no sudo rights and cannot write to /opt/machine-runner-swarm.
  • The job user runs every job step. It is circleci in the cimg images, or the account you name with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER.

The runner steps each job down to the job user with command_prefix: sudo -niHu <job user> -- in the default class, setpriv when the image has no sudo, and always setpriv --no-new-privs in the hardened class. The token is never in the job environment, and the config file that the runner reads is readable only by the runner user and root. In the single-task classes that file holds the placeholder.

MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO decides the rest:

Class type Setting Jobs have sudo Can a job read the class token
Default (linux-default, and linux-java of classes-extra.yaml) "true" Yes, passwordless, as in the Docker executor No, the container holds a placeholder. Only a job that escapes onto the node of the proxy can
Hardened (linux-hardened of classes-extra.yaml) "false" No No, for the same reason
Persistent (linux-persistent, no proxy) "false" (the shipped file; "true" is the opt-in) No (with "true": yes) No, as in the hardened class. With "true", yes if the job uses sudo (The persistent class)

The default class. Jobs keep the passwordless sudo that many orgs and orbs expect, for example sudo apt-get install. A job that uses sudo is root in its container: it can read the placeholder and the files of the runner, and become the runner user, but it finds no class token (linux/tests/proxy.sh scans the containers as root to show it).

The hardened class. The entrypoint steps every job down with util-linux setpriv --no-new-privs, even when the image has sudo, and edits no file of the image. Swarm ignores no-new-privileges, so setuid binaries such as sudo and su stay in the image. The kernel flag that setpriv sets is inherited by the job and everything it starts, and cannot be cleared, so no setuid binary can lift a job to root, even through a local-root bug.

  • The container exits with code 80 if the image has no util-linux setpriv.
  • Jobs cannot install system packages at run time, and nothing in a job gains privileges through setuid or file capabilities (for example ping or mount). Build the tools into the image. CircleCI also recommends pre-installing dependencies as the most secure option.
  • A kernel or container-runtime bug can still lift a job to root, because the containers share the host kernel.

Choose the hardened class for shared or regulated work, and the default class for a single trusted team that needs sudo. See Security.

What the Linux entrypoint does

circleci-runner-entrypoint starts as root, prepares the container, and runs the runner as the runner user. It never reads the token or the placeholder. In order, it:

  1. Waits for the runner distributor, resolves current once, and checks the binary against its SHA-256 record. It also checks that the runner and every directory above it, up to /opt/machine-runner-swarm, are owned by root and not writable by the group or others.
  2. Looks for the tools it needs: sudo or util-linux setpriv to step jobs down, and setpriv or su to start the runner. With MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false, util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs is required. Without the tools it exits with code 80 (What an image needs).
  3. Creates the users with useradd or adduser (sudo refuses a user that has no passwd and no shadow entry): circleci-runner with uid and gid 2000, and the job user when the image has none.
  4. Sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_COMMAND_PREFIX. A value in the service environment does not override it.
    • With sudo, the prefix is ["sudo","-niHu","<job user>","--"]. The file /etc/sudoers.d/90-circleci-runner lets uid 2000 run commands as the job user only, and keeps the PATH and environment variables of the image.
    • Without sudo, or with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false, it is a setpriv command that gives the job no capabilities (in the hardened class also --no-new-privs), run through env -u for every CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_* variable of the container (the runner name stays). The runner holds CAP_SETUID and CAP_SETGID as ambient capabilities only to call it.
  5. Creates the task agent and working directories, adds the job user to the group of /var/run/docker.sock when the class mounts the socket (Docker Builds), and runs the runner with exec as uid 2000. The init process (init: true) passes SIGTERM to it, which starts the runner drain.

It does not validate the runner name, the token, the mode, or the timeouts: the runner checks its own settings and exits with code 80 for a bad one. With sudo, a job gets the environment variables of the image (PATH, JAVA_HOME, LANG), the variables you set in the service (such as a proxy), and CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME, and nothing else from the runner.

Users and the runner token on Windows

Windows containers have no step-down: the runner and the jobs run as ContainerAdministrator, because the runner needs its symbolic link privilege to install the task agent. A job can read the config file of its runner. In a single-task class it holds only the placeholder (the class token is in token-proxy-windows), in the persistent class the real token. The token is not in the job environment. A hostile job on the same host as the proxy can still reach it, because process isolation is not a security boundary (Windows).

Treat each Windows resource class as a trust boundary: one token for each class, restricted users, rotated tokens. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER do not exist on Windows. See Token model on each OS.

Placement

Services carry constraints and nodes advertise capabilities. The built-in properties are node.platform.os and node.platform.arch. This repository adds the node labels machine-runner-swarm.zone, machine-runner-swarm.docker-build, machine-runner-swarm.microvm, machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022, machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025, and machine-runner-swarm.class.<service>. See Multi-Node Clusters.

Why Swarm and not plain Compose

A plain docker compose up restarts the same container, so the environment is not clean. Swarm creates a new container for every task. The FAQ lists the trade-offs.

Glossary

Term Meaning
Stack file A Compose-format YAML file that docker stack deploy reads: a main file (runners.yaml) for each OS and optional add-on stack files. This documentation never calls an add-on stack file an overlay, because an overlay network is a different thing
Stack The services that one docker stack deploy creates, named runners here, so the service linux-default is runners_linux-default in Swarm commands
Resource class, service A resource class is the CircleCI name, <namespace>/<name>, that a job selects with resource_class. A service is the Swarm object that runs it, named like the class without the namespace
runner-bin, current, record runner-bin is the named volume, one on every node, that holds the runner versions under versions/<version>. current is the link to the active version, which a container resolves once at start. The record is versions/<version>/SHA256, the SHA-256 of the binary in sha256sum -c format, which the entrypoint checks at every container start
Runner distributor The global service runner-distributor (Linux) or runner-distributor-windows (it installs portable Git too) that downloads, verifies, and installs the runner into runner-bin, moves current, and looks again every MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL
Drain A runner drain happens when the runner gets SIGTERM: it takes no new job and finishes the running one. A node drain is docker node update --availability drain: Swarm stops the tasks of that node, which starts a runner drain in each, and starts replacements on other nodes. This documentation always says which one
